Subject: Making sense of the breach notice

Hi Nilesh,

Could you check my thinking? The notice from the ticket site says names, email addresses and phone numbers were exposed. It says card details and passwords were not.

So here is what I worked out. Since my phone number and email leaked, I may get fake messages that look like they come from the site, or calls from someone who already knows my name. Someone could also use my details to sound convincing to other people. Since no card was involved, the bank isn't the first priority. The main thing is not to trust unexpected messages, and to ask the site before clicking anything.

Does that sound right?

Payal

qa.q: What did the notice say was exposed?
qa.a: Names, email addresses and phone numbers.

qa.q: Why did Payal write to Nilesh?
qa.a: Payal wanted a second opinion on the reasoning and was a little unsure, so asked for a check before deciding what mattered most.

qa.q: What else could Payal do to act on this reasoning, and why?
qa.a: Payal could tell the people close to Payal that fake messages may arrive, because knowing what leaked helps them spot a trick too.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel on receiving the email?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel trusted and pleased to see careful thinking, and would probably only need to add a small point or two.

grounding: The person reads the notice to see what data leaked, lists possible risks and uses that to decide which steps matter most.

passage:
'We have detected a security incident affecting some customer records.' That's how the email started, Nilesh, and my first instinct was to panic. I'm Gurleen, and I panic efficiently, so instead I read the whole thing twice.
First question: what exactly leaked? Not my password, the notice said. Names, email addresses, phone numbers and delivery addresses. No card details, because they don't store cards.
Second question: so what can someone do with that? I made a list on my phone. They could send emails pretending to be the company. They could call me, knowing my name and address, and sound very convincing. They might try it on my parents too, since it's their home address.
Third: so what matters most? Not changing my card, then. Being careful with calls and messages. So that evening I told Mummy and Papa: if anyone calls about 'your daughter's order', hang up and call me.
Two weeks later a man called Papa, used my name, and asked for an OTP. Papa hung up.

qa.q: What data did the notice say was exposed?
qa.a: Names, email addresses, phone numbers and delivery addresses.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when the email first arrived?
qa.a: Gurleen's first instinct was panic, turned into careful reading instead.

qa.q: Why did knowing what leaked change Gurleen's steps?
qa.a: With no card or password exposed, the real risk was convincing calls and emails, so warning Gurleen's parents mattered most.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when the caller asked for an OTP?
qa.a: Suspicious and alert, and probably relieved that Gurleen had warned him that evening.

grounding: Shows a young person reading a breach notice to see exactly what leaked and listing the likely risks, which decides the steps that matter.

I'm Ishita, and I sit opposite Vaibhav at work. When our health insurer sent a breach notice last month, most of us glanced at it and moved on. Vaibhav read it with a pencil.
He underlined the lines about what was exposed: name, date of birth, policy number, phone number and 'some claim details'. Then he said aloud, mostly to himself, 'So not passwords or cards. But enough to pretend to be me. Or to pretend to be them, calling me.'
He wrote a sticky note. Watch for calls or messages quoting my policy number. Never share an OTP. Call the insurer only on the number on my card. Ask whether anyone can change my contact details without extra checks.
That afternoon he called the insurer on the number printed on his card and asked that last question. They added a verification step to his account.
I can't say whether he was worried. He seemed calm. But the next week, when a caller quoted his policy number, he hung up within ten seconds.

qa.q: What did the notice say was exposed?
qa.a: Name, date of birth, policy number, phone number and some claim details.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been worried about as he underlined the notice?
qa.a: That someone could use his details to impersonate him, or pose as the insurer to trick him.

qa.q: Which item on Vaibhav's sticky note mattered most when the caller quoted his policy number?
qa.a: Never sharing an OTP and calling the insurer only on the number on his card, so he hung up quickly.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav's reaction look to Ishita?
qa.a: Ishita notices how carefully he read the notice while others ignored it, and sees it pay off when the fake call comes.

grounding: Shows a person reading a breach notice to see exactly what was exposed and listing the risks, like impersonation calls, to decide the key steps.
